slides.title: Visual Identity Systems
slides.subtitle: Design without strategy is the Pepsi document. Strategy without design is a Word doc with good intentions. The system is what happens when both are present.

slides.title: Twenty-seven pages about having nothing to say
slides.lead: In 2008 Pepsi paid Arnell Group to tilt a swoosh a few degrees. What leaked was the rationale.
bullets: The document invoked the Golden Ratio, the Mona Lisa, the Parthenon, the Vitruvian Man, the Theory of Relativity, and the gravitational pull of the Earth.
None of that authorized the logo. The logo authorized nothing.
The real diagnosis: **Pepsi's brand had not committed to anything specific enough for the visual to express.** When you have no commitment, you borrow authority.

slides.title: Pepsi, Yahoo, Tropicana
slides.lead: Strategy-free rationale. Strategy-free process. Wrong archetypal foundation. Read them across the same four questions.
slides.why: chapter applies one diagnosis across three named cases — 'Three failure modes. Strategy-free rationale (Pepsi). Strategy-free process (Yahoo). Wrong archetypal foundation (Tropicana).' — and grades craft, commitment, expression and recovery differently for each

slides.title: The damage was legible in the numbers
slides.lead: These are the only figures this chapter states. Everything else in this deck that looks like a number is a slot you have to fill.
bullets: Yahoo published a different logo concept every day for **30 days**, then sold to Verizon in 2017 for **less than $5 billion** — at its peak it had been valued at over **$100 billion**.
Tropicana's repackaging was technically accomplished and expressed the wrong archetype. Sales dropped **20% in two months**. The original packaging was restored.
Every one of the three was avoidable if the design had been required to answer to a prior strategic commitment.

slides.title: "Visual identity" is six things, and they are not independent
slides.lead: Most non-designers treat these as separate decisions. They are a system — each component is perceived in context with the others.
slides.why: chapter enumerates six components and names the sub-items inside each: 'Three structural forms: a wordmark, a symbol, and a lockup'; 'Primary, secondary, and neutral colors'; 'Grid, spacing, and hierarchy rules' — a genuine two-level taxonomy

slides.title: Users do not evaluate components. They form one impression.
slides.lead: Nobody looks at the logo, then separately at the typeface, then separately at the color. They perceive all of it at once.
bullets: That impression either coheres or it conflicts. Users cannot always say what is wrong — they feel it as *the brand is trying to be two things at once*.

Archetypes are the mechanism that makes coherence achievable: components converge **not because each is designed to match the others, but because each is designed to match the same underlying orientation**.
A logo fine in isolation can clash with the wrong typography. A palette beautiful in print can fail accessibility on screen.
The palette is the highest-frequency signal — it appears in every pixel of every interface. Get it wrong and the mismatch is felt on every visit.

slides.title: Sage clarifies. Hero demonstrates. Caregiver embraces. Magician transforms.
slides.lead: Not arbitrary conventions — documented response patterns in how users form impressions.
bullets: **Sage:** restrained, evidence-rich, serif-anchored, generous whitespace, high-contrast type. NYT. The Economist. Stripe's docs. *Sages do not decorate; they clarify.*
**Hero:** bold, saturated, dynamic, diagonal, motion-implying. Nike. Red Bull. *Heroes do not explain; they demonstrate.*
**Caregiver:** warm, approachable, soft-edged, earth tones or pastels. J&J. Headspace. *Caregivers do not challenge; they embrace.*
**Magician:** jewel tones, intentional gradients, unexpected combinations. Early Adobe. Spotify canvas. *The visual should feel like it is already in transition.*

slides.title: Eight sections, each a constraint rather than a description
slides.lead: The creative brief is the only moment where strategy becomes a design requirement before any visual work begins. Without it, decisions are made by taste, made inconsistently, and the system does not cohere.
bullets: Brand strategy summary · project scope · audience · tone words · references · anti-references · constraints · deliverables.
Audience must be named and specific. Not "marketing professionals" — *"marketing managers at small B2B SaaS companies with no dedicated analytics team who will use the tool on Monday mornings."*
"Stripe's documentation site — the way it uses whitespace to make dense technical content feel readable without dumbing it down" is a reference. "I like Stripe" is not.
One to two pages, no padding. **A sentence that cannot be used to evaluate a design decision should be cut.**

slides.title: Vague words are forbidden
slides.lead: Tone words are three to five adjectives that narrow the design space. Most of the words people reach for do not narrow anything.
slides.why: chapter draws an explicit permission boundary around the brief's vocabulary — 'The discipline here is that vague words are forbidden. Innovative, modern, clean, professional are anti-words — they describe nothing, constrain nothing, and could apply to any brand.'

slides.title: The palette starts at the archetype, not at your preference
slides.lead: Colour is the highest-frequency brand signal. A wrong colour decision is encountered more often than any other wrong decision in the system.
bullets: **Sage:** restrained, high-contrast, low-saturation. The neutral system does the heavy lifting; the accent is used sparingly.
**Hero:** saturated primaries, minimal neutrals — the brand lives in the saturated zone. **Caregiver:** earth tones, muted greens, warm grays. **Magician:** jewel tones, gradients, chromatic depth.
Minimum viable palette: **one primary, two accents, two neutrals** — near-black and near-white. A full palette adds one or two mid-neutrals.
For each colour commit a name *and* a hex. The name is for humans; the hex is for implementation. Document both.

slides.title: The numbers are specific and non-negotiable
slides.lead: WCAG 2.2 AA: normal text below 18pt needs 4.5:1. Large text and graphical objects need 3:1. Here is the chapter's own Sage-palette audit, on one axis.
slides.why: chapter publishes a five-row contrast audit with real measured ratios (17.4, 8.9, 8.9, 4.6, 2.9 to 1) against two stated thresholds — magnitudes that belong on one shared axis, with one failure it names and fixes

band.label: passes AA at normal text size

slides.title: Caption failed at 2.9:1. Darken it and it passes at 4.6:1.
slides.lead: The palette's character does not change. The implementation becomes compliant.
bullets: Test *every* combination you intend to use. Document colour name, hex, background hex, ratio, pass/fail.
Small shifts in value bring a failing combination into compliance without changing what the palette feels like.
**WCAG 2.2 AA is a legal requirement in many jurisdictions for public-facing digital products, not a best-practice recommendation.** Document every failure and its resolution before launch.

slides.title: The specification is what prevents drift
slides.lead: Type does the legibility job and the archetype job at once. Choosing two faces is not enough — you have to say how they are used.
slides.why: chapter gives an explicit six-rung type scale as a list block — 'Display / H1: 56px / 1.1 … Caption: 13px / 1.4' — an ordered hierarchy from smallest to largest, and argues 'The specification prevents drift'

slides.title: Same five pages. Different archetype. Different structure.
slides.lead: Home, About, Projects, Writing, Contact. Every page beyond five needs explicit justification. The section order is not neutral — it is an archetype expression.
slides.why: chapter runs one shared origin into two outcomes — 'Produce two wireframe descriptions in structured text for the same five-page portfolio: one for a Sage archetype, one for a Hero archetype. The pages are the same; the section order, density, and component character should differ.'

tracks.label: Sage · leads with the thinking
notes: more text density, fewer full-bleed images

tracks.label: Hero · leads with the image
notes: a metrics strip, then short punchy copy

slides.title: Chapter 6 opened it. This chapter closes it.
slides.lead: The brief turned the strategy into constraints. A palette without a type system is a colour mood board. A type system without a layout system is a font choice. A layout system without an archetype is a default template.
slides.why: chapter states a provenance chain — 'Chapter 6 produced a brand strategy. The creative brief translated that strategy into design constraints. The palette expressed the archetype in colour… the brand guidelines document captures all of those decisions' — and ends with a test whose outcome the reader must run

slides.title: Hand the document to someone who was not there
slides.lead: The grey slot at the end of that chain is the only honest verdict available to me. It is your run, not mine.
bullets: Give the brand guidelines to one classmate uninvolved in your brand work. Ask them to make **one** decision using only the document — a button colour, a headline weight.
Then evaluate whether their choice was archetype-aligned. If it was, the document is specific enough. If it was not, find the gap: vague tone words? a missing palette variant? an unspecified weight?

And be honest about the limit: **the causal evidence that archetype-aligned visual identity moves user trust in AI tools specifically is thin.** The mechanism is plausible and branding-supported; the AI-specific evidence is largely anecdotal and survivor-biased.

slides.title: Coherence is the standard. Craft follows with time.
slides.lead: Write the brief before you open the design tool. Commit a hex and a name for every colour. Measure every contrast ratio instead of estimating it. Then hand your guidelines to a stranger and find out whether the system is a system — or a mood board with confidence.
